title: MVC pattern
description: Model-View-Controller separates data (Model), presentation (View), and input handling (Controller): the controller updates the model, the model notifies the view. Recognizing MVC in code means finding the triangular dependency — views observe models, controllers mutate models, models know nothing of either. Variants (MVP, MVVM) shift where the logic lives, but the separation is the point.
mechanism: Detect: classes with UI rendering + observer registration (Views), classes with business state + notifications (Models), classes wiring input to model updates (Controllers). Dependency rule: View -> Model (observe), Controller -> Model (mutate), never Model -> View directly.
algo: O(classes) classification by role heuristics + dependency direction checks.

title: Layered architecture
description: Layered architecture stacks UI -> application -> domain -> infrastructure, with dependencies pointing strictly downward. Recognizing it means checking the dependency arrows: any upward or skipped-layer edge is a violation. The pattern's strength is replaceability — swap the infrastructure layer without touching the domain — and its weakness is the temptation to skip layers 'just this once'.
mechanism: Assign each module to a layer (by directory, package, or annotation); build the dependency graph; flag edges that go up or skip layers. Metrics: layer cohesion, skip ratio, upward edges (must be zero).
algo: O(V+E) graph check. Layer assignment is the manual step; everything else is automatic.
demo:
# dependency rule: UI -> app -> domain -> infra, never upward
LAYERS = {'ui': 3, 'app': 2, 'domain': 1, 'infra': 0}
edges = [('ui', 'app'), ('app', 'domain'), ('domain', 'infra'),
         ('ui', 'domain'),   # skip: allowed but smelly
         ('infra', 'domain')]  # upward: VIOLATION

for a, b in edges:
    la, lb = LAYERS[a], LAYERS[b]
    verdict = 'ok' if la > lb else ('SKIP (smelly)' if la == lb + 2 else 'VIOLATION (upward)')
    print('%-6s -> %-6s %s' % (a, b, verdict))

title: Microservices detection
description: Microservices show up as independently deployable units with their own datastores, communicating over the network: the tell-tale signs are separate repos/pipelines, no shared database tables, and API contracts between services. Detection mines deployment configs, database access patterns, and network calls. The anti-pattern it guards against is the distributed monolith — network calls with monolithic coupling.
mechanism: Signals: separate deployables, database-per-service (no cross-service table access), synchronous vs async call patterns, independent scaling configs. Score each boundary; flag shared-DB access across services as the top smell.
algo: O(services) signal collection; cross-service DB access is a join over access logs.

title: Event-driven architecture
description: Event-driven systems communicate through events, not calls: producers emit facts ('order placed'), consumers react independently. Recognizing it means finding the event backbone (broker, log) and the publish/subscribe topology. The benefits are decoupling and replayability; the costs are eventual consistency and the debugging difficulty of 'who reacted to this event?'
mechanism: Detect: message broker dependencies, publish/subscribe call sites, event schema registries. Map: event types -> producers -> consumers. Check: schema versioning, dead-letter handling, idempotent consumers.
algo: O(publish/subscribe sites) topology mapping. Consumer idempotency is the correctness property to verify.

title: Dependency analysis
description: Dependency analysis turns imports into a graph and reads the architecture from it: package coupling (afferent/efferent), instability metrics, and cycle detection. Robert Martin's package metrics (I = Ce/(Ca+Ce), abstractness vs instability) quantify what reviewers feel. The analysis is cheap — parse imports, build the graph — and it catches architectural decay before humans notice.
mechanism: Extract imports per module; compute Ca (incoming), Ce (outgoing), I (instability), A (abstractness); plot A vs I (the 'main sequence'); flag cycles and distance-from-sequence outliers.
algo: O(V+E) graph metrics. The main-sequence distance D = |A + I - 1| spots the painful packages.
demo:
# Martin package metrics: instability I = Ce/(Ca+Ce)
# Ca = incoming deps, Ce = outgoing deps
pkgs = {
    'ui': ({'app'}, {'app', 'util'}),       # Ca, Ce as (incoming, outgoing) sets
    'app': ({'ui'}, {'domain', 'util'}),
    'domain': ({'app'}, set()),
    'util': ({'ui', 'app'}, set()),
}
print('%-8s %4s %4s %6s' % ('package', 'Ca', 'Ce', 'I'))
for p, (ca, ce) in pkgs.items():
    I = len(ce) / (len(ca) + len(ce)) if ca or ce else 0
    print('%-8s %4d %4d %6.2f %s' % (p, len(ca), len(ce), I,
          '<- stable, hard to change' if I < 0.3 else '<- unstable, easy to change'))

title: Architecture recovery
description: Architecture recovery reconstructs the intended design from the code as built: cluster modules by dependency patterns, name the clusters, and compare against the documented architecture. The gap between 'as designed' and 'as built' is architectural drift, and recovery makes it visible. Techniques range from simple clustering to topic modeling on identifiers.
mechanism: Dependency graph -> clustering (Louvain, hierarchical); label clusters by dominant terms; diff against the intended architecture map. Drift = edges crossing intended boundaries.
algo: Clustering O(V log V)-ish; labeling by term frequency. The intended map is the human input.
demo:
# recover modules from the dependency graph via simple clustering
import itertools
edges = [('a', 'b'), ('b', 'c'), ('a', 'c'), ('x', 'y'), ('y', 'z'), ('x', 'z'), ('c', 'x')]
# Louvain-lite: start each node alone, merge pairs with the most internal edges
nodes = sorted({n for e in edges for n in e})
clusters = [{n} for n in nodes]

def internal(c):
    return sum(1 for a, b in edges if a in c and b in c)

improved = True
while improved:
    improved = False
    for i, j in itertools.combinations(range(len(clusters)), 2):
        if internal(clusters[i] | clusters[j]) > internal(clusters[i]) + internal(clusters[j]):
            clusters[i] |= clusters[j]
            del clusters[j]
            improved = True
            break
print('recovered clusters:', [sorted(c) for c in clusters])
print('name them, compare to the documented architecture: the gap is the drift')

title: Conformance checking
description: Conformance checking continuously verifies the code obeys the architecture: no UI->DB edges, no cycles, layering intact. Rules are declared (in code or config) and checked in CI on every PR — architecture as executable specification. The alternative is architecture documents that describe a system that no longer exists.
mechanism: Rules: allowed/forbidden dependency edges, layering, naming conventions. Check per PR on the dependency graph diff; fail on new violations; grandfather old ones with a ratchet. Dashboards trend violations over time.
algo: O(changed edges) per PR against the rule set. Ratcheting keeps it about new violations.

title: Service boundary detection
description: Finding service boundaries in a monolith means finding the seams: clusters of code with high internal coupling and low external coupling, aligned with business capabilities. Detection combines dependency clustering with domain-term analysis (ubiquitous language per cluster). The output is a candidate decomposition — seams to cut along — validated by checking that each candidate owns its data.
mechanism: Cluster by dependencies; score candidate boundaries by coupling ratio; check data ownership (tables touched per cluster); align with domain terms. Human validates: the algorithm proposes, architects dispose.
algo: Clustering + coupling metrics; data-ownership check is a join over access logs.
demo:
# candidate service boundaries: high internal, low external coupling
internal = {('a', 'b'): 9, ('b', 'c'): 8, ('x', 'y'): 7}   # calls within candidate
external = {('c', 'x'): 1}                                  # calls across
cands = {'svc1': {'a', 'b', 'c'}, 'svc2': {'x', 'y'}}

def cohesion(nodes):
    inn = sum(v for (a, b), v in internal.items() if a in nodes and b in nodes)
    ext = sum(v for (a, b), v in external.items() if (a in nodes) != (b in nodes))
    return inn / (inn + ext) if inn + ext else 0

for s, nodes in cands.items():
    print('%s cohesion %.2f %s' % (s, cohesion(nodes), '(clean seam)' if cohesion(nodes) > 0.8 else ''))
print('cut along high-cohesion seams; each service must own its data')

title: Monorepo patterns
description: Monorepos keep all services in one repository with shared tooling: atomic cross-service changes, one version of everything, unified CI. The patterns that make it work are sparse checkouts (clone what you need), build graph awareness (only build affected), and code ownership (CODEOWNERS per directory). Detection-wise, the monorepo is visible in the build graph and the ownership map.
mechanism: Build graph (Bazel/Buck) defines the real module structure; ownership files define review responsibility; CI uses affected-analysis to test only impacted targets. Visibility rules replace version boundaries.
algo: Affected analysis O(build graph) per change; sparse checkout O(needed files).

title: Pattern catalogs
description: A pattern catalog documents the recurring solutions — name, problem, solution, consequences — so teams choose consciously instead of reinventing. The Gang of Four catalog is the famous one; every organization grows its own (our API pattern, our worker pattern). Detection tools can check conformance to catalog patterns: 'this looks like our Repository pattern but bypasses the unit of work'.
mechanism: Catalog entries: name, intent, structure (roles), consequences, examples. Detectors match structural roles against the catalog; linters flag near-misses. Catalogs live in the repo, versioned with the code.
algo: Structural matching per pattern; the catalog is documentation with teeth when checkers enforce it.
demo:
CATALOG = {
    'Repository': {'intent': 'abstract data access', 'roles': ['interface', 'impl', 'entity'],
                   'rule': 'callers use the interface, never the impl'},
    'Worker Pool': {'intent': 'bounded concurrency', 'roles': ['queue', 'workers', 'results'],
                    'rule': 'workers >= 1; queue bounded'},
}
for name, p in CATALOG.items():
    print('%-12s intent: %s' % (name, p['intent']))
    print('             roles: %s' % p['roles'])
    print('             rule : %s' % p['rule'])
print('name, problem, solution, consequences: choose consciously, not by accident')

title: Anti-pattern pairs
description: Every pattern has an evil twin: the Singleton's twin is global state, the microservice's is the distributed monolith, caching's is cache-aside-without-invalidation. Recognition means spotting the shape and naming the twin — 'this is not a service, it is a distributed monolith: it has network calls AND shared-database coupling'. Pairs make reviews concrete instead of hand-wavy.
mechanism: For each pattern, document its anti-pattern twin with detection signals. Review checklists ask the twin question: 'is this actually X, or X-shaped Y?' Detectors flag the twin's signals.
algo: Signal-based detection per twin; the value is in naming, which focuses the fix.
demo:
TWINS = [
    ('Microservice', 'Distributed monolith', 'network calls + shared DB tables'),
    ('Cache', 'Stale cache', 'no invalidation on writes'),
    ('Singleton', 'Global state', 'mutable + globally reachable'),
    ('Event-driven', 'Event soup', 'no schema registry, unknown consumers'),
]
print('%-14s %-20s signal' % ('pattern', 'evil twin'))
for p, t, s in TWINS:
    print('%-14s %-20s %s' % (p, t, s))
print('name the twin: reviews get concrete, fixes get focused')

title: Architecture visualization
description: Architecture diagrams generated from code stay honest: dependency graphs rendered per layer, with violations highlighted, regenerated on every commit. The best views are hierarchical (package -> module -> file, drill-down) and diffable (what changed architecturally in this PR?). A diagram drawn once in a wiki rots; a diagram generated from the build is always current.
mechanism: Dependency graph -> layout (layered/graphviz) -> render with violation overlays. Drill-down by zooming the hierarchy. Diff: graph delta between commits, rendered as added/removed edges.
algo: Layout O(V+E); rendering the changed subgraph only keeps it fast.
demo:
# architecture as data: render the layer graph, highlight violations
LAYERS = {'ui': 0, 'service': 1, 'db': 2}
edges = [('ui', 'service'), ('service', 'db'), ('ui', 'db')]

print('layer diagram (generated from imports, every commit):')
for layer in sorted(set(LAYERS) | {b for _, b in edges}, key=lambda l: LAYERS.get(l, 9)):
    outs = [b for a, b in edges if a == layer]
    marks = ['%s%s' % (b, ' !!' if LAYERS.get(b, 9) < LAYERS.get(layer, 9) - 1 else '') for b in outs]
    print('  [%s] -> %s' % (layer, ', '.join(marks) or '(nothing)'))
print('!! = violation overlay: the diagram shows the rot, not just the design')

title: Refactoring guidance
description: Pattern recognition should end in action: 'this cluster wants to be a service; cut here, own this data, expose this API'. Guidance ranks refactorings by payoff (coupling reduced per effort) and sequences them (break the cycle before extracting the service). The output is a backlog, not a report — each item with the seam, the data to own, and the first safe step.
mechanism: Score candidate refactorings by (coupling_delta / effort); order by dependencies (prerequisites first); emit as tickets with context. Re-run after each refactoring to re-rank — the landscape changes.
algo: O(candidates) scoring; re-rank O(candidates) after each change.
demo:
# rank refactorings by payoff: coupling reduced per unit effort
cands = [
    ('break ui<->db edge', 9, 2),
    ('extract billing service', 20, 8),
    ('split util package', 6, 3),
]
ranked = sorted(cands, key=lambda c: c[1] / c[2], reverse=True)
print('%-24s %8s %8s %8s' % ('refactoring', 'payoff', 'effort', 'ratio'))
for name, pay, eff in ranked:
    print('%-24s %8d %8d %8.1f' % (name, pay, eff, pay / eff))
print('do the top item first; re-rank after each: the landscape changes')

title: Fitness functions
description: Architecture fitness functions are automated checks that the architecture keeps its promises — 'no cycles', 'p99 under 200ms', 'services own their data' — run in CI like tests. Neal Ford's term for executable architecture: the build fails when the design degrades. Fitness functions turn 'we have a layered architecture' from a claim into a continuously verified fact.
mechanism: Functions: structural (dependency rules), behavioral (performance budgets), data (ownership). Run in CI; trend over time; alert on degradation, not just violation. Each maps to an architectural decision record (ADR).
algo: O(checks) per CI run. Trending needs the history — store results per commit.

title: Tooling for pattern detection
description: Pattern detection tooling spans from lint rules (cheap, local) to full architecture platforms (expensive, global): import-linters for layering, ArchUnit for Java rules-as-tests, Structure101/CodeScene for visualization and trends. The pragmatic stack is layered too — fast local checks in the editor, deep analysis in CI, trends on the dashboard. One tool rarely covers all three speeds.
mechanism: Editor: instant local rules. CI: full-graph checks on the PR. Dashboard: trends and drift over months. Same rule definitions, three runtimes.
algo: O(changed) locally; O(graph) in CI; O(history) for trends.
demo:
STACK = [
    ('editor', 'import-linter', 'O(changed): instant feedback as you type'),
    ('ci', 'ArchUnit / deptrac', 'O(graph): full rules on every PR'),
    ('dashboard', 'CodeScene', 'O(history): drift trends over months'),
]
print('%-10s %-18s %s' % ('where', 'tool', 'cost'))
for where, tool, cost in STACK:
    print('%-10s %-18s %s' % (where, tool, cost))
print('same rules, three runtimes: fast local, deep CI, trending dashboard')
